propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of a decision dated October 23, 2013, refusing reconsideration of a danger opinion under the Act.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of a decision of Citizenship and Immigration Canada, dated October 23, 2013, wherein the Director, Case Determination, appointed as the Minister’s delegate (the delegate), refused the applicant’s request for reconsideration of the Minister’s opinion issued against him on November 10, 2010, stating that he constitutes a danger to the public under paragraph 115(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [the Act].

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of a 2013 decision refusing reconsideration of a danger opinion under the Act.

propositions.text: The applicant seeks to set aside the decision and have the matter redetermined by a different delegate.
propositions.quote: The applicant seeks an order setting aside the decision and returning the matter to a different delegate for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant seeks to set aside the decision and have the matter redetermined by a different delegate.

propositions.text: The applicant is a Pakistani citizen who entered Canada in 1993 claiming refugee status.
propositions.quote: The applicant is a citizen of Pakistan. In October 1993, he entered Canada at the port of Vancouver and claimed refugee status.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a Pakistani citizen who entered Canada in 1993 claiming refugee status.

propositions.text: The applicant became a permanent resident as a Convention refugee in 1996.
propositions.quote: On May 9, 1996, the applicant became a permanent resident as a Convention refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant became a permanent resident as a Convention refugee in 1996.

propositions.text: In 2001, an inadmissibility report for serious criminality was issued after the applicant's aggravated assault conviction; he received a warning letter.
propositions.quote: On February 2, 2001, an inadmissibility report for serious criminality was issued against the applicant following his conviction for aggravated assault. He was issued a warning letter.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that in 2001 an inadmissibility report was issued after the applicant's aggravated assault conviction and he was warned.

propositions.text: In 2004, an inadmissibility report was issued after 2001 drug trafficking convictions; a deportation order was issued and appealed.
propositions.quote: On January 28, 2004, an inadmissibility report for serious criminality was issued against the applicant following his convictions in 2001 for trafficking in a controlled substance. A deportation order was consequently issued. The applicant filed an appeal to the Immigration Appeal Division of the Immigration Refugee Board.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that in 2004 an inadmissibility report and deportation order were issued after 2001 drug trafficking convictions, and the applicant appealed.

propositions.text: In 2007, an inadmissibility report was issued after drug-related convictions.
propositions.quote: On August 30, 2007, an inadmissibility report for serious criminality was issued against the applicant following his 2007 drug related convictions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that in 2007 an inadmissibility report was issued after drug-related convictions.

propositions.text: In 2008, a deportation order for serious criminality was issued against the applicant.
propositions.quote: On July 7, 2008, a deportation order for serious criminality was issued against the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that in 2008 a deportation order for serious criminality was issued against the applicant.

propositions.text: On November 10, 2010, the applicant was found to be a danger to Canada and not at risk if removed to Pakistan.
propositions.quote: On November 10, 2010, the applicant was found to be a danger to Canada pursuant to subsection 115(2)(a) of the Act and not at risk if removed to Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the applicant a danger to Canada and not at risk if removed to Pakistan in 2010.

propositions.text: In 2012, the applicant requested reconsideration of the danger opinion, submitting a new statutory declaration about his criminal involvement.
propositions.quote: On November 14, 2012, the applicant made a request for reconsideration of his danger opinion. The submissions included a new statutory declaration from him, which details his involvement in criminal matters.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker notes the applicant requested reconsideration in 2012 with new statutory declaration about criminal involvement.

propositions.text: The delegate refused the applicant's request for reconsideration of the danger opinion in 2013.
propositions.quote: In a decision dated October 23, 2013, the delegate refused the applicant’s request for reconsideration of the Minister’s opinion issued against him on November 10, 2010, stating that he constitutes a danger to the public under paragraph 115(2)(a) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker refused the applicant's request for reconsideration of the danger opinion in 2013.

propositions.text: The delegate found the applicant inadmissible for serious criminality based on convictions in 2000, 2001, and 2007.
propositions.quote: First, the delegate conducted the danger assessment. The delegate found that the applicant is inadmissible for serious criminality under paragraph 36(1)(a) of the Act, based on his convictions in 2000, 2001 and 2007.

propositions.text: The delegate found the applicant's criminal activities serious and dangerous, with lack of meaningful rehabilitation despite efforts.
propositions.quote: The delegate found that the applicant’s criminal activities were both serious and dangerous to the public and that there is a lack of evidence of meaningful rehabilitation despite his efforts to pursue education and upgrade his skills.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate found the applicant inadmissible for serious criminality and lacking meaningful rehabilitation despite efforts.

propositions.text: The delegate found the applicant minimized his role in crimes, but noted positive factors like compliance and rehabilitation efforts.
propositions.quote: The delegate noted that the applicant’s explanation of his role in the criminal offences differs from the Court’s transcript and this demonstrates an attempt to minimize his role in the crimes. The delegate observed some positive factors, such as the applicant’s compliance with the conditions of release, his participation in rehabilitative programming and his efforts to improve his employment opportunities.

propositions.text: Ultimately, the delegate found the applicant a present and future danger to the public; new evidence did not change this.
propositions.quote: Ultimately, the delegate found that, on a balance of probabilities, the applicant represents a present and future danger to the Canadian public. It was determined that the new evidence presented by the applicant did not lead the delegate to a different decision.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate found the applicant minimized his role but noted positive factors; still found him a present and future danger; new evidence did not change decision.

propositions.text: The risk assessment tests if the applicant would face persecution, risk to life, or cruel treatment if removed to Pakistan.
propositions.quote: The delegate noted that the test is whether the applicant, “if removed to Pakistan, will personally face a risk of persecution, risk to life or risk of torture or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.”

propositions.text: The applicant claimed his house was firebombed in Pakistan and he is targeted by TTP due to his brother's political involvement.
propositions.quote: The applicant stated in his request for reconsideration that in July 2011, his picture was in the paper because his house was firebombed and burned in Pakistan. In submissions dated May 16, 2013, the applicant stated he has become a target of the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) due to his brother’s political involvement.

propositions.text: The applicant claimed a poster of him as a TTP target was placed on a mosque wall.
propositions.quote: He claimed there is a poster of him placed on the wall of his mosque as a TTP target.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate stated the risk test if removed to Pakistan; the applicant claimed house firebombed and TTP targeting due to brother's politics.

propositions.text: The delegate considered new evidence: FIR related to 1993 arrest warrant, MQM-Haqiqi risk, PPP death threats, and TTP hit list targeting applicant and brother.
propositions.quote: The delegate considered the following new evidence and the risks alleged by the applicant: a First Information Request (FIR) possibly related to the 1993 arrest warrant issued against the applicant; the risk from the MQM-Haqiqi faction; death threats to his family from the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP), which was suspected to be behind the house burning; and the risk due to his brother’s political involvement which resulted in the TTP naming both him and his brother on a hit list, as evidenced by their picture on a poster outside a mosque.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate considered new evidence including FIR, MQM-Haqiqi risk, PPP death threats, and TTP hit list targeting applicant and brother.

propositions.text: The delegate gave little weight to the FIR due to contradictions and reliance on UK report about falsified documents.
propositions.quote: Insofar as the FIR is concerned, the delegate gave it little weight. The delegate first summarized the circumstances in Pakistan which led to the applicant’s refugee claim. The delegate stated that the 1993 arrest warrant was included as an exhibit during the refugee hearing. The applicant also provided a copy of a FIR dated May 1, 1990 detailing him as one of three leaders of a violent demonstration. The delegate noted the circumstances described in the FIR and determined they are similar to the basis of the 1993 arrest warrant; however, the Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative described an event taking place on May 5, 1991, over one year later. The delegate found there is a lack of clarity regarding the sequence of events. The UK Border Agency’s Country of Origin Report - Pakistan (2004 UK Report) dated June 18, 2004, was then reviewed and the delegate stated that most of the documents presented by asylum seekers were falsified. Relying on this report and the contradiction between the dates, the delegate gave the FIR little weight.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate gave little weight to the FIR due to contradictions and UK report on falsified documents.

propositions.text: The delegate found the risk from MQM-Haqiqi faction low due to applicant's prolonged absence and lack of high profile.
propositions.quote: Insofar as the risk from the MQM-Haqiqi faction is concerned, the delegate found that the risk is low. The delegate acknowledged that, at the time the applicant left Pakistan, he was a high ranking active member of the MQM and the MQM-Haqiqi had an interest in him. It found, however that given the applicant’s prolonged absence from Pakistan and a lack of continued high profile as an active member of the MQM, the applicant would not likely be a target. The delegate drew support from the most recent 2013 UK Country of Origin Information Report detailing the political landscape in Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate found the risk from MQM-Haqiqi faction low due to applicant's prolonged absence and lack of high profile.

propositions.text: The delegate found insufficient evidence that the applicant's home was deliberately targeted in the firebombing.
propositions.quote: With respect to the newspaper article about the burning of the applicant’s home in Qasba Colony, the delegate found that there is insufficient evidence to establish that his home was deliberately targeted.

propositions.text: The delegate noted the Daily Ummat News Karachi is one of many newspapers and that articles can be paid for, citing the 2004 UK Report.
propositions.quote: The delegate first observed a report from a CIC analyst who prepared the Request for Minister’s Opinion on April 10, 2013, noting the Daily Ummat News Karachi is one of 141 newspapers published in Sindh Province. The delegate stated that, according to the 2004 UK Report, it is possible to pay to have a newspaper article published depicting a situation of persecution.

propositions.text: The delegate found insufficient evidence to conclude the house was deliberately targeted based on the article.
propositions.quote: The delegate found that there was insufficient evidence on file to lead him or her to conclude that the applicant’s house was deliberately targeted.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate found insufficient evidence that the applicant's home was deliberately targeted, noting paid newspaper articles and lack of proof.

propositions.text: The delegate found the applicant's usual Pashto language decreases weight of his claim to Muhajir community membership.
propositions.quote: Also, the delegate found that the fact that the applicant normally speaks Pashto “decreases the weight of his submission that he is a member of the Muhajir community.”

paragraphs.summary: The delegate found the applicant's usual Pashto language decreases weight of his claim to Muhajir community membership.

propositions.text: The delegate found photos of applicant and brother with political figures do not indicate MQM allegiance.
propositions.quote: With respect to the risk allegedly faced by the applicant due to his brother’s political involvement, two types of evidence were submitted: photographs and hit posters. The delegate found that photographs of him and his brother with political figures at what appears to be a public event are not indicative of his and his brother’s allegiance to the MQM.

propositions.text: The delegate found the TTP threat credible but unlikely to target the applicant due to prolonged absence.
propositions.quote: In light of the applicant’s prolonged absence, the delegate found that, although the threat of violence from the TTP is credible, the applicant would not likely be a target.

propositions.text: The delegate found the hit posters not authentic as they used passport-style photos.
propositions.quote: Regarding the hit posters, the delegate noted that “hit list” photos are typically taken during meetings, at public events or from news articles; however, the photos on the posters are passport-style photos of the applicant and his brother. The delegate held that the posters are not authentic.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate found photos do not show MQM allegiance, TTP threat credible but unlikely to target applicant, and hit posters not authentic.

propositions.text: Delegate discussed violence in Karachi and MQM's involvement in human rights abuses and opposition targeting.
propositions.quote: The delegate referenced excerpts from documentary evidence and acknowledged the state of violence in Karachi and that the MQM has been blamed for human rights abuses.

propositions.text: Delegate found possibility of risk from general violence does not outweigh danger applicant poses to Canada.
propositions.quote: this mere possibility of risk due to the general violence in Karachi, a city of over 11 million people, does not, in my opinion, outweigh the danger that Mr. Ahmed poses to the public in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate acknowledged violence in Karachi and MQM's abuses but found general violence risk does not outweigh danger Ahmed poses to Canada.

propositions.text: Delegate found applicant not at risk from alleged arrest warrant in Pakistan.
propositions.quote: The delegate found that he is not at risk due to an alleged outstanding arrest warrant against him in Pakistan.

propositions.text: Delegate acknowledged possible arrest at airport if warrant exists.
propositions.quote: if the warrant exists, the applicant could be arrested at the airport upon his return.

propositions.text: Delegate found applicant unlikely subject of 1993 arrest warrant due to passport application and travel since 1993.
propositions.quote: the delegate found that the applicant is not likely the subject of an arrest warrant from 1993, as shown by his ability to apply for a passport in his own name and his unrestricted travel into and outside of Pakistan since 1993.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate found Ahmed not at risk from arrest warrant, noting his passport application and travel since 1993.

propositions.text: Delegate found applicant would not face risk to life, liberty or security on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: the delegate found the applicant would not personally face a risk to life, liberty or security of the person on a balance of probabilities.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate found Ahmed would not face personal risk to life, liberty or security on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Delegate found applicant not established enough in Canada to suffer disproportionate hardship if removed.
propositions.quote: the delegate found that the applicant has not demonstrated a degree of establishment in Canada that would cause him disproportionate hardship should he be removed.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate found Ahmed not sufficiently established in Canada to suffer disproportionate hardship if removed.

propositions.text: Delegate concluded need to protect Canadian society outweighs risks applicant might face if returned to Pakistan.
propositions.quote: the delegate determined that the need to protect Canadian society outweighs the possible risks that the applicant might face if returned to Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The delegate concluded protecting Canadian society outweighs risks Ahmed might face if returned to Pakistan.

propositions.text: Did the delegate err by relying on outdated evidence?
propositions.quote: Did the delegate err by relying on outdated evidence?

propositions.text: Did the delegate exceed his or her jurisdiction?
propositions.quote: Did the delegate exceed his or her jurisdiction?

paragraphs.summary: The applicant raises issues whether the delegate erred by relying on outdated evidence and exceeded jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Applicant has not shown serious or arguable legal issue for application success.
propositions.quote: the applicant has not demonstrated that there is a serious or arguable issue of law upon which the proposed application might succeed.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues applicant has not shown a serious or arguable legal issue for success.

propositions.text: Issues rephrased as standard of review, reasonableness of risk assessment, jurisdiction, and proper assessment steps under Act.
propositions.quote: I would rephrase the issues as follows: A. What is the standard of review? B. Was the delegate’s risk assessment reasonable? C. Did the delegate exceed his or her jurisdiction? D. Did the delegate follow the proper steps for the assessment under paragraph 115(2)(a) of the Act?

paragraphs.summary: The court rephrases issues as standard of review, reasonableness of risk assessment, jurisdiction, and proper assessment steps.

propositions.text: Delegate erred by relying on outdated 2004 IRB document 'Fraudulent Documents'.
propositions.quote: the delegate erred in relying on outdated documents in forming its decision. He argues that the delegate relied heavily on an Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) document, “Fraudulent Documents.” This document reports that it is possible to pay for a newspaper article to be published depicting a situation of persecution. It dates back to 2004.

propositions.text: 2011 IRB document now part of current National Documentation Package for Pakistan.
propositions.quote: a 2011 IRB document now forms part of the current standard National Documentation Package for Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the delegate erred relying on outdated 2004 IRB document, noting a 2011 IRB document is current.

propositions.text: 2011 IRB document shows some newspaper articles and FIRs may be fraudulent due to poor police techniques, not falsified documents.
propositions.quote: The 2011 IRB document indicates that “some newspaper articles may be fraudulent” and estimates that one to five percent of the reports made by Pakistan’s 100,000 newspapers are false. It also notes that some FIRs may be “fraudulent”. However, the applicant contends that a reading of the document reveals that “fraud” is not a matter of falsified documents, but rather reflects police officers’ poor forensic and investigatory techniques and low ethical standards.

propositions.text: Current evidence indicates different situation than 2004 report.
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that the current evidence indicates a different situation than that which existed in 2004.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues 2011 IRB document shows fraud reflects poor police work, indicating a different situation than 2004 report.

propositions.text: Delegate's reliance on 2004 report was reviewable error for avoiding risk analysis and discounting submissions.
propositions.quote: the delegate used this information to completely avoid analyzing the risk that the applicant faces due to the outstanding arrest warrant and to discount his submission of risk.

propositions.text: Delegate highlighted FIR date discrepancy despite 2011 report showing errors in genuine FIRs.
propositions.quote: the delegate highlighted the discrepancy in dates between the FIR and the applicant’s testimony during his refugee claim, even though the 2011 report shows that, even in genuine cases, there might be errors in FIRs.

propositions.text: Delegate relied on 2004 report about paid newspaper articles but ignored 2011 report stating practice less frequent.
propositions.quote: the delegate relied on the 2004 report to find that “it is possible to pay to have a newspaper article published depicting a situation of persecution” while ignoring the statement in the 2011 report that this practice has become less frequent.

propositions.text: Delegate's use of outdated report prejudiced applicant.
propositions.quote: the delegate used this outdated report in a manner that prejudiced him.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues delegate's reliance on 2004 report was error that prejudiced him by avoiding risk analysis and ignoring updated evidence.

propositions.text: Delegate exceeded jurisdiction by reassessing elements essential to refugee status, contrary to Nagalingam.
propositions.quote: the delegate exceeded its jurisdiction by going behind a refugee determination to disprove elements that were essential to the initial grant of refugee protection.

propositions.text: Nagalingam states delegate's role is not to remove or alter refugee status in danger opinion assessment.
propositions.quote: Under Nagalingam v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FCA 153 at paragraph 43, [2009] 2 FCR 52 [Nagalingam], a delegate’s role in assessing a danger opinion is not to “remove or alter the subject’s status as Convention refugee.”

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues delegate exceeded jurisdiction by reassessing refugee status elements, contrary to Nagalingam ruling.

propositions.text: Delegate found applicant not Muhajir despite IRB acceptance, undermining political affiliation claims.
propositions.quote: the delegate made a finding that the applicant is not a Muhajir, even though the applicant’s identity was accepted by the IRB and was central to its finding that he had refugee status.

propositions.text: Delegate used Pashto language finding to doubt MQM membership claim.
propositions.quote: The delegate found that Pashto, one of the languages the applicant normally speaks, “decreases the weight of his submission that he is a member of the Muhajir community.”

propositions.text: Delegate refused to accept prior criminal record and FIR from Pakistan.
propositions.quote: The delegate also erred in refusing to accept the applicant’s prior criminal record and FIR from Pakistan.

propositions.text: Delegate exceeded jurisdiction by reassessing refugee status elements, preventing proper risk analysis.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the delegate exceeded its jurisdiction by attempting to reassess key elements of the applicant’s refugee status. This error prevented the delegate from properly analyzing whether the applicant’s status might place him at risk in Pakistan as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues delegate wrongly reassessed refugee status elements, undermining identity and risk analysis, exceeding jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Delegate made fundamental errors in risk determination regarding outstanding arrest warrant.
propositions.quote: the delegate made fundamental errors in determining that the applicant was not at risk due to an outstanding arrest warrant in Pakistan.

propositions.text: Delegate discounted criminal charge due to outdated documentation.
propositions.quote: The delegate discounted his outstanding criminal charge because he or she concluded that the FIR was not genuine based on outdated documentation.

propositions.text: Delegate cited no evidence that passport cannot be issued with outstanding charge.
propositions.quote: the delegate did not cite any evidence that led him or her to conclude that an individual cannot be issued a passport if he or she has an outstanding criminal charge.

propositions.text: 2012 UK report states accused persons not barred from passports unless central government orders.
propositions.quote: the documentary evidence and specifically, the 2012 UK Country of Origin Information Report relied on by the delegate, notes the contrary: “even a person that was the accused in multiple FIRs would not be barred from obtaining a passport unless the central government had specifically ordered that a passport not be issued to him or her … .”

propositions.text: Delegate erred in risk assessment due to ignoring brother's political profile.
propositions.quote: the delegate erred in determining that he is not at risk for his political association due to his prolonged absence and lack of high profile because the delegate ignored the evidence that his brother is still in the public eye for his political activities with the MQM.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues delegate erred in risk assessment, discounting arrest warrant, ignoring passport evidence, and brother's political profile.

propositions.text: Delegate improperly conflated distinct steps of danger opinion process per Nagalingam.
propositions.quote: the applicant submits that the delegate improperly conflated distinct steps of a danger opinion. He cites Nagalingam for the steps the delegate ought to take under the proper process.

propositions.text: Delegate failed to properly balance risk of Karachi violence against danger posed by applicant.
propositions.quote: even after the delegate accepted the evidence that Karachi is a dangerous city, he or she failed to engage in a proper balancing of that risk against the danger posed by the applicant.

propositions.text: Delegate concluded without step-by-step analysis.
propositions.quote: The delegate came to a conclusion without doing a step-by-step analysis.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues delegate conflated danger opinion steps and failed proper risk balancing, concluding without stepwise analysis.

propositions.text: Applicant does not contest inadmissibility for serious criminality under Act.
propositions.quote: the applicant does not contest the finding that he is inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality under paragraph 36(1)(a) of the Act.

propositions.text: Main issues are delegate's factual findings on risk evaluation and balancing risk with protecting Canadian society.
propositions.quote: the two main issues are the delegate’s factual findings with respect to i) risk evaluation; and ii) the balancing of any risk with the need to protect Canadian society.

propositions.text: Delegate's factual conclusions are reviewable on reasonableness standard (Nagalingam).
propositions.quote: It states the two main issues are the delegate’s factual findings with respect to i) risk evaluation; and ii) the balancing of any risk with the need to protect Canadian society. It submits that the delegate’s factual conclusions are reviewable on the standard of reasonableness (Nagalingam at paragraph 32).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent notes applicant does not contest serious criminality inadmissibility; delegate's findings reviewed for reasonableness.

propositions.text: Delegate's analysis was thorough and reasonable; microscopic approach cautioned against (Ragupathy).
propositions.quote: the delegate’s analysis was thorough and reasonable and that the applicant is asking this Court to adopt a microscopic approach to the delegate’s decision. The Federal Court of Appeal cautions against this approach in Ragupathy v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FCA 151 at paragraph 15, [2007] 1 FCR 490 [Ragupathy].

propositions.text: Hasan outlines process for determining danger opinion; applicant must establish current risk or hardship.
propositions.quote: The respondent cites Hasan v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 1069 at paragraph 10, [2008] FCJ No 1342 [Hasan], for the process of determining a danger opinion. It submits that, although the applicant challenges the delegate’s analysis for steps four and five, it is ultimately the applicant’s onus to establish current risk or hardship.

propositions.text: Applicant cannot rely solely on Convention refugee status to establish risk or hardship (Hasan).
propositions.quote: The applicant cannot simply rely upon his status as a Convention refugee (Hasan at paragraph 22).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues delegate's analysis reasonable; applicant must prove current risk, not rely on refugee status alone.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted new FIR dated May 1, 1990, naming him leader of violent demonstration.
propositions.quote: the FIR dated May 1, 1990, which names the applicant as one of three leaders of a violent demonstration, is new evidence that the applicant submitted at his reconsideration request.

propositions.text: Delegate reasonably examined new FIR evidence with applicant's submissions and IRB hearing information.
propositions.quote: The delegate reasonably examined this evidence in the context of the applicant’s submissions and the available information at the time of the IRB refugee hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent states applicant submitted new FIR evidence; delegate reasonably examined it with submissions and IRB info.

propositions.text: Applicant challenges weight, not discrepancies, of FIR as identified by delegate.
propositions.quote: the applicant does not challenge the discrepancies in dates as identified by the delegate, but rather challenges the weight the delegate gave to the FIR.

propositions.text: Delegate did not err relying on 2004 report as it was contemporaneous to arrest warrant and FIR dates.
propositions.quote: the delegate did not err by relying on the 2004 report because, unlike the 2011 report, it was more contemporaneous to the dates of the applicant’s purported arrest warrant of 1993 and the 1990 FIR.

propositions.text: Delegate reasonably found 2011 article was published at applicant's request to further interests.
propositions.quote: As for the 2011 news article in the Daily Ummat, the delegate was reasonable to find that this article was published at the applicant’s request to further his interests, given the availability of fraudulent documents and the significant period of his absence.

propositions.text: Delegate reasonably found applicant's prolonged absence and lack of high profile decreases likelihood of being targeted.
propositions.quote: The delegate reasonably found that in light of the applicant’s prolonged absence and a lack of demonstrated continued high profile as an active member of the MQM, the applicant has a decreased likelihood of being a target of opposition party members.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues delegate reasonably relied on 2004 report, found 2011 article was self-serving, and applicant's absence reduces targeting risk.

propositions.text: Delegate acknowledged risk of arrest at airport but found applicant unlikely subject of 1993 warrant due to passport and travel.
propositions.quote: The delegate also acknowledged the risk of the applicant’s return as a deportee and the possibility of him getting arrested at the airport. However, it reasonably found that he is not likely still the subject of an arrest warrant from 1993 as shown by his ability to apply for a passport in his own name and his unrestricted travel into and outside of Pakistan since 1993.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent states delegate acknowledged arrest risk but reasonably found applicant unlikely subject of 1993 warrant due to passport and travel.

propositions.text: The 2012 UK report notes many FIRs are baseless and passport issuance is not prevented without central government order.
propositions.quote: the respondent argues that this report also notes that many FIRs are baseless and the registration of FIRs does not prevent the issuance of a passport unless specifically ordered by the central government.

propositions.text: The government did not order passport prevention, suggesting no interest in the applicant.
propositions.quote: Here, the government did not issue such an order, which suggests that it is not interested in the applicant.

propositions.text: The delegate properly noted the applicant’s submission about his brother’s political profile.
propositions.quote: The delegate also properly noted the applicant’s submission about his brother’s purported political profile.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues the 2012 UK report shows many FIRs are baseless and no passport order was issued, and the delegate noted the brother's political profile.

propositions.text: The delegate reasonably gave no weight to submissions about the TTP and found insufficient evidence of targeting.
propositions.quote: The respondent notes that the delegate was reasonable to give no weight to the applicant’s submissions about the TTP and to find that there was insufficient evidence to conclude that the applicant, his brother and his family were targets of the TTP.

propositions.text: The delegate acknowledged TTP as credible threat but reasonably concluded applicant unlikely targeted due to limited MQM involvement since 1993.
propositions.quote: While the delegate acknowledged that the TTP was a credible threat to some groups in Pakistan, the delegate reasonably concluded that the applicant would not likely be targeted because of his limited involvement in the MQM since 1993.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent says delegate reasonably gave no weight to TTP submissions and found applicant unlikely targeted due to limited MQM involvement.

propositions.text: The delegate did not exceed jurisdiction and considered applicant’s Convention refugee status and new evidence thoroughly.
propositions.quote: the respondent submits that the delegate did not exceed its jurisdiction. Here, the delegate took into consideration the applicant’s status as a Convention refugee. In the context of the new evidence, the delegate thoroughly considered each area of risk raised by the applicant.

propositions.text: The delegate did not go behind the applicant’s refugee status but assessed risk on current record.
propositions.quote: The delegate did not go behind the applicant’s status as a Convention refugee in the analysis. The delegate assessed his risk based on the current record.

propositions.text: There was no indication the 1990 FIR was submitted to the IRB.
propositions.quote: Here, there was no indication that the 1990 FIR was submitted to the IRB.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent submits delegate did not exceed jurisdiction, considered refugee status and new evidence, and no indication 1990 FIR was before IRB.

propositions.text: The delegate’s danger opinion was reasonable, balancing public danger against risk to applicant.
propositions.quote: the respondent submits that the delegate’s danger opinion was reasonable. The delegate appropriately assessed the risk to the applicant should he return and balanced the danger to the public against the degree of any risk.

propositions.text: Delegate found applicant inadmissible for serious criminality, criminal activities serious and dangerous, present and future danger to public, and no risk if removed on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: the delegate found that: i. the applicant was inadmissible for serious criminality; ii. his criminal activities were both serious and dangerous to the public; iii. he represented a present and future danger to the Canadian public; and iv. if removed from Canada, he would not face a risk to life, liberty or security of the person on a balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: This shows delegate considered all possible risks.
propositions.quote: The respondent argues this demonstrates that the delegate considered all possible risks.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent submits delegate’s danger opinion was reasonable, found applicant inadmissible and dangerous, and considered all risks.

propositions.text: Respondent has not supported that redetermining refugee claim aspects would not exceed delegate’s jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: The applicant submits that the respondent has not provided support for the conclusion that the redetermination of key aspects of the applicant’s refugee claim would not improperly exceed the delegate’s jurisdiction.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits respondent failed to support that redetermining refugee claim aspects would not exceed delegate’s jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Delegate made negative plausibility findings on brother’s political affiliation without documentary evidence, which should only occur in clearest cases.
propositions.quote: he argues that the delegate made negative plausibility findings regarding the applicant’s brother’s political affiliation. These findings should only be made in the clearest of cases. Here, the delegate did not provide any documentary evidence in support of this conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues delegate made unsupported negative plausibility findings on brother’s political affiliation, which require clearest cases.

propositions.text: Respondent erred by applying risk assessment under sections 96 and 97 of the Act instead of section 7 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: the applicant submits that the respondent erred in noting the requirements of risk assessments pursuant to sections 96 and 97 of the Act; rather, risk should be assessed pursuant to section 7 of the Charter which comprises risk beyond the scope of sections 96 and 97 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits respondent erred by applying risk assessment under sections 96 and 97 of Act instead of section 7 of Charter.

propositions.text: Where jurisprudence has resolved standard of review, analysis need not be repeated (Dunsmuir).
propositions.quote: Where the jurisprudence has satisfactorily resolved the standard of review, the analysis need not be repeated (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at paragraphs 45, 47, 48, 49, 53, 57 and 62, [2008] 1 SCR 190).

paragraphs.summary: Court states that where jurisprudence has resolved standard of review, analysis need not be repeated (Dunsmuir).

propositions.text: Delegate’s factual findings reviewed on reasonableness standard with high deference (Nagalingam).
propositions.quote: In Nagalingam at paragraph 32, the Federal Court of Appeal found that the factual findings of a delegate should be reviewed on a standard of reasonableness and a high degree of deference should be afforded.

paragraphs.summary: Nagalingam holds delegate’s factual findings reviewed on reasonableness standard with high deference.

propositions.text: Reasonableness means decision must be transparent, justifiable, intelligible and within acceptable outcomes (Dunsmuir).
propositions.quote: The standard of reasonableness means that I should not intervene if the Board’s decision is transparent, justifiable, intelligible and within the range of acceptable outcomes (Dunsmuir at paragraph 47).

propositions.text: Court will set aside decision only if reasons or facts supporting outcome are not understandable (Newfoundland Nurses).
propositions.quote: Here, I will set aside the Board’s decision only if I cannot understand why it reached its conclusions or how the facts and applicable law support the outcome (Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 at paragraph 16, [2011] 3 SCR 708).

propositions.text: Court reviewing for reasonableness cannot substitute own view or reweigh evidence (Khosa).
propositions.quote: As the Supreme Court held in Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paragraphs 59 and 61, [2009] 1 SCR 339, a court reviewing for reasonableness cannot substitute its own view of a preferable outcome, nor can it reweigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains reasonableness standard and limits on judicial review (Dunsmuir, Newfoundland Nurses, Khosa).

propositions.text: Court will first address Issue 3.
propositions.quote: I wish to first deal with Issue 3.

paragraphs.summary: Court states it will first address Issue 3.

propositions.text: Applicant claims delegate exceeded jurisdiction by going behind Refugee Board’s finding that applicant was Mohajir and MQM member.
propositions.quote: The applicant claims that the delegate exceeded his or her jurisdiction by going behind the findings of the Refugee Board which had found that the applicant was a Mohajir and a member of the MQM.

propositions.text: Delegate stated applicant’s Record of Landing shows Pashto as mother tongue, MQM represents Urdu-speaking Mohajir community, and applicant’s Pashto use decreases weight of Mohajir membership submission.
propositions.quote: The delegate stated in the decision: Mr. Ahmed’s Record of Landing indicates that his mother tongue is Pashto. The documentary evidence indicates that the MQM represents the mostly Urdu-speaking Mohajir community, originally Indian Muslims who fled to Pakistan following the 1947 partition. Mr. Ahmed has indicated that he speaks Urdu in other immigration documents and, based on his participation in his refugee hearing using an Urdu interpreter, I do believe that he is fluent in Urdu, the official language of Pakistan. However his indication that Pashto is one of the languages he normally speaks decreases the weight of his submission that he is member of the Muhajir community.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant claims delegate exceeded jurisdiction by rejecting Refugee Board’s finding applicant was Mohajir and MQM member; delegate noted Pashto mother tongue.

propositions.text: Delegate disagreed with Board’s finding on applicant’s identity as Mohajir and MQM member.
propositions.quote: The above statement by the delegate indicates to me that the delegate disagreed with the Board’s finding as to the identity of the applicant as a Mohajir and a member of the MQM.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds delegate disagreed with Board’s finding on applicant’s identity as Mohajir and MQM member.

propositions.text: Nagalingam states section 115 requires non-refoulement to apply until exceptions engaged; delegate must not rule on refugee status but on acts depriving benefits.
propositions.quote: In Nagalingam, the Federal Court of Appeal states at paragraphs 41 to 43: 41 Respectfully, I find that Justice Kelen ignored the structure of section 115, as well as Canada’s overall responsibilities with regards to the Convention, when finding that the absence of risk for the appellant, if returned to Sri Lanka, was determinative of his right to non-refoulement. 42 The scope of section 115 is such that the principle of non-refoulement continually applies to a protected person or a Convention refugee until one of the two exceptions listed therein is engaged. Thus, to determine that the principle of non-refoulement no longer applies simply because the conditions in the protected person’s or the Convention refugee’s country of origin have improved is to short-circuit the process. 43 The approach of Justice Kelen essentially forces the Delegate to act beyond his jurisdiction, ruling on the appellant’s status as a Convention refugee, rather than whether the nature and severity of the acts committed deprive him of the benefits associated with that status (i.e. not to be refouled). To this end, I agree with the respondent that the Ragupathy approach ensures that the Delegate maintains his jurisdiction as his role is not in any way to remove or alter the subject’s status as Convention refugee (respondent’s memorandum at paragraph 71). Proceeding in this manner guarantees that the Delegate’s function will not usurp the role of the Refugee Protection Division on a cessation determination pursuant to subsection 108(2) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Nagalingam holds section 115 requires non-refoulement until exceptions apply; delegate must not rule on refugee status but on acts depriving benefits.

propositions.text: Section 115 of the Act prohibits removal of protected persons to countries where they face persecution or risk of torture, with exceptions for serious criminality or security risks.
propositions.quote: For ease of reference, section 115 of the Act reads as follows: 115. (1) A protected person or a person who is recognized as a Convention refugee by another country to which the person may be returned shall not be removed from Canada to a country where they would be at risk of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion or at risk of torture or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. 115. (1) Ne peut être renvoyée dans un pays où elle risque la persécution du fait de sa race, de sa religion, de sa nationalité, de son appartenance à un groupe social ou de ses opinions politiques, la torture ou des traitements ou peines cruels et inusités, la personne protégée ou la personne dont il est statué que la qualité de réfugié lui a été reconnue par un autre pays vers lequel elle peut être renvoyée. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply in the case of a person (2) Le paragraphe (1) ne s’applique pas à l’interdit de territoire : (a) who is inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality and who constitutes, in the opinion of the Minister, a danger to the public in Canada; or a) pour grande criminalité qui, selon le ministre, constitue un danger pour le public au Canada; (b) who is inadmissible on grounds of security, violating human or international rights or organized criminality if, in the opinion of the Minister, the person should not be allowed to remain in Canada on the basis of the nature and severity of acts committed or of danger to the security of Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Court recites section 115 of the Act prohibiting removal of protected persons except for serious criminality or security risks.

propositions.text: Delegate exceeded jurisdiction by not accepting IRB’s finding that applicant was Mohajir and MQM member; decision unreasonable and must be set aside.
propositions.quote: In my view, the delegate exceeded his or her jurisdiction by not accepting the IRB’s finding that the applicant was a member of the Muhajir community and a member of the MQM party. The delegate then used his finding to deny the applicant’s request. I find that this was unreasonable and as a result, the decision must be set aside and returned to a different delegate for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds delegate exceeded jurisdiction by rejecting IRB’s finding on applicant’s identity; decision unreasonable and set aside.

propositions.text: Due to finding on jurisdiction, court need not address other issues.
propositions.quote: Because of my finding on this issue, I need not deal with the other issues.

paragraphs.summary: Court will not address other issues due to jurisdiction finding.

propositions.text: Responses to information requests dated December 13, 2011 were not before delegate and should not be part of record.
propositions.quote: The respondent requested that since the responses to information requests dated December 13, 2011 were not before the delegate, it should not be part of the record. I agree.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees responses to December 13, 2011 information requests were not before delegate and should be excluded.

propositions.text: Neither party submitted a proposed serious question of general importance for certification.
propositions.quote: Neither party wished to submit a proposed serious question of general importance for my consideration for certification.

paragraphs.summary: Neither party submitted a serious question of general importance for certification.
